narrative: You are being denied a promotion because the model estimated a 90% chance that you will leave the organization. In practical terms, it sees you as highly likely to exit soon, so it treats promotion as a retention investment unlikely to pay off. This prediction was driven most strongly by your overall years of experience, then by whether you have other job opportunities, and then by your tenure in your current organization. All three pushed the model toward “will leave.” Your 6–10 years of overall experience was the strongest signal; among employees predicted to stay, most had only 1–5 years, so your longer track record appears to the model as greater mobility. You also reported having other job opportunities, which is a strong flight-risk signal, especially since only about a quarter of stayers reported the same. Your 1–5 years in your current organization was the third-ranked factor and further increased the leave estimate, even though this tenure length is common among stayers. Before revisiting promotion, you and your manager should discuss your career path, pay concerns, recognition, workload, job stability, and whether those outside opportunities can be addressed. The organization should treat this as a retention conversation, not a final judgment, and document concrete commitments and a review date.
